title: William Rowan Hamilton and the Invention of Quaternions (1843)
explainer: Hamilton discovered the quaternion number system in 1843 while walking along a Dublin canal, carving the formula i²=j²=k²=ijk=−1 into a bridge stone on the spot. Modern game engines use unit quaternions instead of raw Euler angles to represent 3D rotations because they interpolate smoothly and avoid gimbal lock, the orientation-math glitch that plagues naive camera rigs and skeletal animation. Knowing where this four-dimensional algebra came from makes the 'why quaternions, not just matrices' design choice in engines like Unity and Unreal feel less like arbitrary magic.

title: Binary Space Partitioning and the Making of Doom (1993)
explainer: Binary space partitioning trees were developed by researchers including Bruce Naylor in the early 1980s as a general way to order surfaces for rendering, but John Carmack adopted the technique for id Software's Doom to solve a very specific problem: keeping frame rates playable on 1993-era PCs by precomputing which walls could hide others. That choice let Doom, and later Quake, skip huge amounts of redundant rendering work at runtime, and BSP-style spatial partitioning is still a direct ancestor of the visibility and culling systems in modern game engines. It's a clear case of academic graphics research crossing over into an industry it wasn't originally built for.
